title: Words you may confuse
subtitle: quite / quiet, lend / borrow, fell / felt
summary: Keep apart the words elementary learners most often mix up - quite and quiet, lose and loose, lend and borrow.

left.label: quite
left.text: One syllable. It means 'a little, but not very'. It rhymes with *right*.

right.label: quiet
right.text: Two syllables. It means 'silent, with very little sound'. It rhymes with *higher*.
examples: Please be **quiet**. The baby is sleeping.
It's very **quiet** here in the evening.

left.label: lose
left.text: A verb. If you **lose** something, you do not know where it is. It rhymes with *shoes*.
examples: Why do I always **lose** my keys!
If you **lose** your passport you must call the embassy.

right.label: loose
right.text: An adjective. Clothes that are **loose** are not tight - they are too big. It rhymes with *juice*.
examples: Do you have this skirt in a smaller size? This one is too **loose**.

lesson.heading: fell / felt and cook / cooker
lesson.text: **Fell** is the past of *fall*. **Felt** is the past of *feel*. A **cook** is a person; a **cooker** is the machine you cook on.

examples.text: Yesterday I **fell** and broke my arm.
I **felt** ill yesterday, but I feel OK today.

left.label: lend
left.text: You **give** something to someone for a short time.

right.label: borrow
right.text: You **get** something from someone for a short time.
examples: Can I **borrow** your camera for two hours?
Sometimes I **borrow** books and DVDs from friends.

lesson.heading: check and control
lesson.text: To **check** something is to look at it to see if it is right. To **control** something is to tell it what to do.

examples.text: We use the mouse to **control** the computer.

lesson.heading: wait, hope and expect
lesson.text: We **wait for** a bus or a person. We **hope** for something we really want. We **expect** something we think is probable, even if it is bad news.

examples.text: I haven't studied; I **expect** I'll fail my exams.
I'm **expecting** my brother at 5.30. He said he would come.

lesson.heading: afternoon, evening and night
lesson.text: In English the **afternoon** is from about 12 o'clock till 5 or 6 pm. The **evening** is from 5 or 6 pm until about 9 or 10 pm. After that it is the **night**.

examples.text: We say *Good **night*** when we go to bed.

lesson.text: Remember the rhymes: *quite* rhymes with *right*, but *quiet* rhymes with *higher*.
